{"id": "89:27/q03", "question": "Who utters the address?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine address is direct or delivered through angels.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q03/p1", "position": "God addresses the believer directly, honoring the soul.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, Rāzī, al-Nasafī, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compare God's speech to Moses; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows direct speech in a fresh passage. Quṭb describes an intimate call from the highest assembly."}, {"id": "89:27/q03/p2", "position": "An angel speaks God's address to the soul.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān takes this as apparent; the Abū Bakr reports explicitly mention an angel. Al-Qurṭubī says angels address God's friends. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers leaving the speaker unrestricted to include both possibilities."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q04", "question": "What does nafs denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether it denotes the whole person, self, spirit, or a kind of substance.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q04/p1", "position": "Nafs is the person or continuing self, the 'I' of experience.", "reasons": "Rāzī says awareness of self persists through bodily change and when one is unaware of the body; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 39:56 and 6:151 for the whole person. Elmalılı describes unified awareness, its perceiving and perceived aspects, and God's grounding of that unity in 8:24."}, {"id": "89:27/q04/p2", "position": "Nafs is the spirit that animates the natural or bodily soul.", "reasons": "Tustarī distinguishes life-giving spirit from natural soul. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 12:53; Elmalılı cites 17:85 and 39:42, treating death and sleep as withdrawal, not annihilation. Qushayrī mentions spirit settled toward the still soul."}, {"id": "89:27/q04/p3", "position": "The soul is immaterial, distinct from the body.", "reasons": "Some cited by Rāzī infer this from knowing the self without noticing the body; Rāzī refers to an objection in Lubāb al-Ishārāt. On this account, coming and returning mean assuming and relinquishing bodily governance."}, {"id": "89:27/q04/p4", "position": "The soul is a subtle, luminous celestial body.", "reasons": "Others cited by Rāzī say its attachment animates the body and its departure leaves it dead; on this view coming and return are literal."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q05", "question": "How is muṭmaʾinna derived and what is its basic sense?", "turns_on": "The proposed root order and the basic sense of composure.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q05/p1", "position": "It is an active participle meaning calm, settled, firm, and untroubled.", "reasons": "Rāzī defines iṭmiʾnān as settledness and firmness; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the participle's calmness. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls it a heart verb, surveying eight uses: hearts reassured in 3:126, 8:10, 13:28, and 2:260, and safety in 16:112 and 4:103; bodily calm depends on inner calm."}, {"id": "89:27/q05/p2", "position": "Its root has hamza first and mīm second.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers Abū ʿAmr's analysis of the radical order."}, {"id": "89:27/q05/p3", "position": "It derives by metathesis from ṭaʾmana.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Sībawayh's derivation, yielding muṭaʾminna and iṭmiʾnān, citing 2:260 and 4:103."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q06", "question": "What makes this soul tranquil?", "turns_on": "Whether tranquility rests on affirmed revelation, certainty, safety, remembrance, contentment, divine knowledge, or another state.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q06/p1", "position": "It is a believing soul, assured by God's words, promise, reward, and resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as believing; Qatāda and al-Ḥasan say it affirms God's words. Al-Ṭabarī specifies promise of afterlife honor; al-Farrāʾ and Kufan grammarians add reward and resurrection. Al-Wāḥidī unites the glosses under God's promise. The Prophet's taught prayer adds belief in meeting God and acceptance of decree."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p2", "position": "It possesses settled certainty of God and truth, free from doubt.", "reasons": "Mujāhid adds recognition of God as Lord and firm obedience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya regards this as certainty beyond faith with no remaining question, comparing Abraham in 2:260; Rāzī and others cite the same verse. Al-Ālūsī calls this a good interpretation and links remembrance to understanding in 13:19 or 39:9."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p3", "position": "It is safe from fear, grief, and punishment.", "reasons": "Ubayy's reading adds āmina, 'secure'; al-Kalbī glosses that as believing. Rāzī cites the angelic reassurance of 41:30. Al-Biqāʿī adds freedom from loss and disappointment grounded in worldly belief in the Hereafter. The security may be realized at death, resurrection, or Paradise."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p4", "position": "It rests through remembrance of God.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī and others cite 13:28. Rāzī prefers this on Qurʾānic and rational grounds: reason ascends causes to the Necessary Existent, while limitless human needs require God's limitless perfection. Al-Bayḍāwī and Elmalılı repeat the proofs."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p5", "position": "It is content with God's decree, reward, and gifts.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says it knows whatever misses or reaches it was decreed. Al-Dāmghānī cites 22:11 and 16:106 for iṭmaʾanna as contentment. Al-Ḥasan describes mutual contentment at death; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this prevents pride in blessing and ingratitude in poverty."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p6", "position": "It is humble, repentant, obedient, and devoted to God.", "reasons": "Mujāhid describes resolution in obedience and humble submission; Qāshānī describes certainty illumining the soul. Elmalılı connects this with 8:2, 22:34–35 and 39:54; the soul is free from bondage to desire and acts sincerely with life and wealth."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p7", "position": "It is a knowing soul intimate with God and unable to bear separation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ makes gnosis and longing central. Rāzī says it knows God for God alone and is intimate, longing, alive, and speaking with Him; this account requires advanced intellectual or spiritual attainment. Qushayrī names gnosis as a source of tranquility."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p8", "position": "It is reassured by glad tidings of Paradise at death and later stages.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, Zayd b. Aslam, and the report through Usāma name death, resurrection, and gathering; al-Kalbī and Abū Rawq add a brightened face and the record in the right hand. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows good tidings before entry."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p9", "position": "It is sincere and purified, with blameworthy traits removed.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān glosses it as sincere; Ibn Kathīr calls it purified and aligned with truth. Jurjānī says the heart illuminates it, removing blameworthy traits and bringing out praiseworthy ones."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p10", "position": "It is a soul attached to worldly life and summoned to leave it.", "reasons": "Some spiritual interpreters take the tranquility as worldly complacency; the summons redirects it to God and the afterlife. Rāzī and al-Ālūsī contrast worldly rest with rest in knowledge and worship."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p11", "position": "It is morally steadfast through prosperity and hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it sees both conditions as tests and maintains servitude. Iṣlāḥī says it gives thanks and others' rights in ease and perseveres in adversity; Kur'an Yolu emphasizes revering divine commands and compassion toward creation."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p12", "position": "It is joined to the Real and rests in God's decree.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim says the spirit was adorned and made ready for return; Junayd says God clothes it with guidance until it becomes self-reproaching. A Sufi description derives it from primordial light and directs it solely to witnessing God."}, {"id": "89:27/q06/p13", "position": "It no longer commands evil.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib's gloss is reported by Bint al-Shāṭiʾī; the Study Quran distinguishes the tranquil soul controlling desire from the self-reproaching and evil-commanding states."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q07", "question": "What does the adjective contribute to the address?", "turns_on": "Whether it praises and assures known addressees or identifies a restricted group.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q07/p1", "position": "It praises and reassures those addressed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says souls would not know they qualified before admission, so the adjective explains the good news. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says predicating calm of the soul stresses its inner essence."}, {"id": "89:27/q07/p2", "position": "It identifies the tranquil souls as a particular group.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr allows that God may inspire souls to recognize their tranquility, enabling a restrictive adjective."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q08", "question": "When is the soul addressed?", "turns_on": "Whether the address comes at death, resurrection, after judgment, entry to Paradise, or throughout life.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q08/p1", "position": "At death, as the believer's soul leaves the body.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says this; the Abū Bakr report places the angelic saying at death. Al-Ḥasan describes mutual divine and human satisfaction then. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Zayd b. Ḥārithah and Abū Ṣāliḥ; Elmalılı says return then means the spirit leaving the body."}, {"id": "89:27/q08/p2", "position": "At resurrection, when souls return to their bodies.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and others understand a literal return; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the body is figuratively its lord or owner and connects the scene with 89:21. Al-Biqāʿī places it at the trumpet and graves opening."}, {"id": "89:27/q08/p3", "position": "After reckoning, when judgment is complete.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī judges this most likely; Elmalılı prefers it from context despite death-time reports, reconciling them by treating death as an individual's resurrection or taking the commands as a unit."}, {"id": "89:27/q08/p4", "position": "Upon entry into Paradise.", "reasons": "Several exegetes list this stage; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says at certain entry."}, {"

id": "89:27/q08/p5", "position": "At death and again at resurrection, or at three stages.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr states death and resurrection; Zayd b. Aslam names death, resurrection, and gathering as recurring glad tidings. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ leaves the timing unrestricted to cover all possibilities."}, {"id": "89:27/q08/p6", "position": "It also addresses the tranquil soul throughout worldly life.", "reasons": "Elmalılı calls this reading clearer and more useful; the future divine saying prepares believers for the final day while their tranquility is already formed by faith and good deeds."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q09", "question": "To whom does the address apply, and which occasions are reported?", "turns_on": "Whether a reported individual is exclusive or an instance of a general address.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q09/p1", "position": "It applies generally to every sincere, obedient believer.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Farrāʾ report a general application; al-Qurṭubī prefers it. Al-Kashshāf finds the general reading apparent; al-Nasafī invokes general wording over a particular occasion. Al-Ālūsī treats named persons as illustrations, not limits."}, {"id": "89:27/q09/p2", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr.", "reasons": "Reports say he admired the recited verse and the Prophet foretold that the words, sometimes specified as an angel's, would be said to him at death; variants have him read it to the Prophet or people say it. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ālūsī give no grading."}, {"id": "89:27/q09/p3", "position": "It was revealed concerning ʿUthmān.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk connects it to ʿUthmān purchasing and dedicating the well of Rūma for public water; Ibn ʿAbbās is also cited for the identification."}, {"id": "89:27/q09/p4", "position": "It was revealed concerning Ḥamza after martyrdom at Uḥud.", "reasons": "Burayda and Abū Hurayra are cited. Al-Thaʿlabī says his soul was honored until its return to his body."}, {"id": "89:27/q09/p5", "position": "It was revealed concerning Khubayb ibn ʿAdī.", "reasons": "While crucified by Meccans, he prayed to face the qibla; God turned his face and none could turn it back. Some accounts call him Ḥabīb; these are name variants."}, {"id": "89:27/q09/p6", "position": "The soul is identified as the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to make this identification; al-Ālūsī treats it as illustrative of the general address."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q10", "question": "What is reported at Ibn ʿAbbās's burial?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q10/p1", "position": "A strange bird entered his bier at Ṭāʾif and the verses were recited at his grave by an unseen speaker.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. Jubayr is cited repeatedly; the bird was not seen leaving. Some reports mention the full verses and others this verse alone."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q11", "question": "What happens to a believer's soul at death in the cited reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q11/p1", "position": "Angels welcome it with Paradise's gift and fragrance, then it is placed among believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar or Ibn ʿAmr is named in variants: fragrant departure, opened heavenly doors, angels' prayers, prostration, and a spacious lit grave contrast with the disbeliever's stench, wrath, and Hell. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ describes two angels and musk scent; al-Ḥasan adds entry among the righteous."}, {"id": "89:27/q11/p2", "position": "It sees its place in Paradise and returns to the body for questioning.", "reasons": "Muḥammad b. Kaʿb says it returns pleased with its reward until Munkar and Nakīr question it."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q12", "question": "What other incident is reported with recitation of this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q12/p1", "position": "A severed martyr's head recited it in Roman lands.", "reasons": "Qubāth b. {"id": "89:27/q13", "question": "What supplication is taught for a tranquil soul?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q13/p1", "position": "The Prophet taught prayer for a soul at peace in God, believing in meeting Him, accepting His decree, and content with His gift.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma transmits it; Ibn Kathīr notes Abū Sulaymān b. Zabr's remark that Rawāḥa's report is unique. Variants say provision or gift."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q14", "question": "How does the soul's tranquility relate to other states of the self?", "turns_on": "How many states there are and how they are ordered.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q14/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān names the evil-commanding, self-reproaching, and tranquil states.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 91:7, 5:116, 32:17, 12:53, 75:2. The Study Quran says desire rules the first, struggles in the second, and is controlled in the third. Elmalılı contrasts earlier worldly and belatedly reproachful souls with timely understanding."}, {"id": "89:27/q14/p2", "position": "Sufi writers enumerate seven states of the soul.", "reasons": "Elmalılı lists commanding, self-reproaching, tranquil, content, accepted, inspired, and purified and relates self-knowledge to knowledge of God. Al-Ālūsī mentions three stations in this passage: tranquil, content, approved."}, {"id": "89:27/q14/p3", "position": "Guidance can move the tranquil soul into self-reproach.", "reasons": "Junayd says God clothes it in guidance until it becomes a self-reproaching soul."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q15", "question": "How does this address connect with the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "How the positive address relates to prior warning and descriptions of worldly life.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q15/p1", "position": "It contrasts the believing soul's good end with worldly regret and punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say the discourse turns to believers. Al-Qurṭubī contrasts trust with wealth-based accusations against God; al-Biqāʿī sees an answer to the fate of the restless miser. Ibn ʿĀshūr says promise after warning encourages good and deters evil. Qutb stresses intimacy amid terror; Iṣlāḥī contrasts gratitude and patience with pride and despair."}, {"id": "89:27/q15/p2", "position": "Its calm recalls the oath's worship times and anticipates the positive ending.", "reasons": "Neuwirth says those times embody trust and calm nearness; Elmalılı likens the righteous life to the ten nights before Eid and entry into Paradise to the festival dawn."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q16", "question": "How does the wording present the address?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted divine saying or a direct standalone call explains its abruptness.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q16/p1", "position": "An omitted 'God says' introduces a future, effective divine address.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the omission intensifies contrast with 89:24. Al-Qaffāl treats the imperative as declarative: the tranquil soul returns. Elmalılı says the majority infer an omitted divine saying and regard the commands as creative rather than legislative."}, {"id": "89:27/q16/p2", "position": "The abrupt direct call honors and reassures the believer now.", "reasons": "Elmalılı allows a direct legislative call at the sūra's close; Kur'an Yolu says its warmth brings future happiness into present life. Ibn ʿĀshūr considers a fresh passage."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q17", "question": "Does this passage belong to the original revelation sequence?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing address was revealed together with the preceding verses or added later.", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q17/p1", "position": "Its placement suggests one sequence with the preceding warnings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the context puts the speech in the afterlife; if the named occasions imply a Medinan verse, it would be separate and placed here by instruction or thematic affinity. He notes the agreed Meccan classification except a report from al-Dānī."}, {"id": "89:27/q17/p2", "position": "Verses 27–30 are a later addition to the sūra.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the positive afterlife ending expands an earlier threat-only unit, pairs Garden with 89:23's Hell, and uses direct speech to supersede negative human statements; 23–24 and 27–30 enact the oath's duality."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q18", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting Sūrat al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q18/p1", "position": "Recitation during the ten nights brings forgiveness; at other times, light on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf transmits this as a Prophetic report."}]}

{"id": "89:27/q21", "question": "How are the following descriptions of contentment parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q21/p1", "position": "Rāḍiyatan and marḍiyyatan are simultaneous circumstantial descriptions.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says neither necessarily entails the other."}]}

{"id": "89:27/q23", "question": "How are these verses used in funeral devotion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q23/p1", "position": "They are prominent in Muslim funeral eulogies.", "reasons": "The Study Quran adds that Sufis see them as describing the purified soul's true nature."}]}
{"id": "89:27/q24", "question": "What closing prayer does Elmalılı offer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:27/q24/p1", "position": "He prays for himself and readers to return content and accepted, join God's sincere servants, and reach Paradise and the vision of God.", "reasons": ""}]}
{"id": "89:28/q01", "question": "Where is the soul told to return?", "turns_on": "The readings differ over whether 'return' addresses a departing spirit, a spirit rejoining its body, an honored arrival at God's reward, or a spiritual turning.", "positions": [{"id": "89:28/q01/p1", "position": "To its body at resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others explain the return as re-entry into the body. Al-Tabari prefers it because 89:29–30 immediately command entry among the servants and into the Garden. Ibn Abbas's singular 'My servant' and Ibn Masud's 'body of My servant' support it (Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi); Sa'id describes souls returning from a river beneath the Throne. Muhammad ibn Ka'b instead locates bodily return after the believer sees Paradise at death, before Munkar and Nakir."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p2", "position": "To God's promised reward, honor, nearness, mercy, or Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Farra places the reward after receipt of the record in the right hand; al-Hasan and many others gloss 'Lord' by His prepared reward. Ibn Ashur describes Paradise as God's honored home, citing 54:55, and says this is a special homecoming earned by good deeds. Al-Alusi mentions the promise of Garden and righteous company, comparing 28:85; his prior-residence explanation through Adam's loins depends on a disputed identification of Adam's Garden."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p3", "position": "To God at death, through the soul's departure from earthly life.", "reasons": "Abu Salih separates this departure from the later entry commands at resurrection. Al-Tustari describes an afterlife path; Ibn Zayd says the spirit returns to a sacred realm. Al-Farra also allows a return from worldly life."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p4", "position": "To the appointed meeting, command, or station of divine care.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi allows the appointed death or resurrection. Al-Alusi describes a blessed waiting station before reckoning, from which the soul returns after judgment; alternatively God's command or general favor follows the barzakh or the period before judgment. Al-Biqa'i identifies the meeting with the Creator at resurrection."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p5", "position": "To God inwardly, by turning from worldly attachment or anxiety about deeds.", "reasons": "The people of indication and al-Bursawi call the soul away from settled worldly life. Al-Alusi and Elmalili describe post-reckoning release from anxiety over accepted deeds; Elmalili also applies the command to voluntary submission in every earthly matter. Al-Alusi rejects a further reading that applies all commands throughout earthly life."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p6", "position": "To the divine Essence beyond the attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani makes completion of the attributes precede return to the Essence and cites 5:119; the Study Quran reports two levels of contentment, through God and before God. Al-Razi describes intellect rising through contingent beings and causes to the Necessary Existent."}, {"id": "89:28/q01/p7", "position": "To the righteous human peers of the soul.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysan glosses 'your Lord' as the soul's peers among God's righteous servants."}]}
{"id": "89:28/q02", "question": "When is this address made?", "turns_on": "The notes place the command at death, revival, judgment, several of these stages, or in the believer's present life.", "positions": [{"id": "89:28/q02/p1", "position": "At death.", "reasons": "Abu Salih reserves entry among the servants and into Paradise for resurrection; the report to Abu Bakr names an angel at death. Ibn Amr's account of a fragrant soul and a lit grave elaborates the departure. Muhammad ibn Ka'b locates a return to the body after a glimpse of Paradise and before questioning."}, {"id": "89:28/q02/p2", "position": "At resurrection, as souls rejoin bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari prefers this in light of the following entry commands. Al-Dahhak says souls approach God as first created; Ibn Ashur connects the scene to the crushed earth in 89:21."}, {"id": "89:28/q02/p3", "position": "After resurrection and completed reckoning.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi places the call when the blessed return from judgment to honor or turn from concern over deeds; Elmalili prefers this as most apparent from the context of 89:24, although he also favors a worldly application elsewhere."}, {"id": "89:28/q02/p4", "position": "Across death, resurrection and gathering, with repeated good news.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam and another report say Paradise is announced at all three moments. Ibn Kathir says the call comes at death and again at resurrection. Al-Tabatabai takes the address as spanning revival to Paradise, or death to entry into the eternal Garden."}, {"id": "89:28/q02/p5", "position": "As an exhortation during worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as an address to believers to persist and strive; Elmalili prefers its continuing practical application. Al-Alusi rejects a particular inward application extending all following commands through worldly life."}]}
{"id": "89:28/q03", "question": "How does the imperative 'return' function?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative is declarative promise, future command, or present exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "89:28/q03/p1", "position": "It can state an already accomplished return or promised state.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and Kufan grammarians liken it to telling an existing tribesman to 'be Tamimi or Qaysi'; after the soul reaches reward the command reports that it is pleased and accepted.
